title: Google and Epic Drop Their Legal Campaign — Android Opens to Rival App Stores July 22
summary: Google will open its Play Store catalog to competing Android app stores in the United States starting July 22 — the direct result of a 2024 injunction that Google spent nearly two years trying to soften or avoid. The last attempt to modify the injunction's structural remedies collapsed this week, when Google and Epic jointly withdrew the motion and Google reaffirmed it will comply.
body:
The waiting is over. Starting July 22, third-party Android app stores in the US will gain access to Google Play's catalog — the result of a 2023 jury verdict and the 2024 injunction it produced that Google spent the better part of two years trying to escape or modify.

On July 15, Google and Epic Games filed a joint withdrawal of their motion to modify the remedies in the Play Store injunction, according to MLex, a specialist legal and regulatory trade wire. The filing stated that Google "will continue to comply with the permanent injunction issued by US District Judge James Donato."

That injunction flows from a December 2023 jury verdict finding Google had unlawfully monopolized Android app distribution. Judge Donato issued the structural remedy injunction in 2024. The Ninth Circuit upheld it on July 31, 2025.

**The road to here — settlement, not exhaustion.** Google's appellate campaign came to an end not because the courts shut every door, but because Google chose to close them. Google filed a stay application at the Supreme Court (docket 25A354) in September 2025; SCOTUS denied the stay on October 6. Google then filed a certiorari petition (docket 25-521) on October 27, 2025. That petition was voluntarily dismissed on March 9, 2026, by joint stipulation under Rule 46 — as part of a broader negotiated settlement announced in November 2025. Under that deal, Google agreed to commissions between 9 and 20 percent for Epic apps, and agreed to admit rival stores, including the Epic Games Store, as approved Android app stores globally. Google gave up its cert petition as part of a deal it chose to strike, not because the Court denied it.

**What was withdrawn this week — and what was not.** The motion that Google and Epic dropped on July 15 was separate from the settlement's financial and global-store terms. It was a bid to *modify the injunction's structural remedies* — the operational requirements attached to Judge Donato's 2024 ruling on US Play Store access. Withdrawing it means those structural requirements remain intact. "Give up fighting" is defensible shorthand: Google exhausted its stay application, voluntarily dropped its cert petition in exchange for a deal, and has now also dropped the remedy-modification motion while reaffirming compliance with the standing injunction.

**What happens July 22.** Under the Play Catalog Access program, Google Play will make its app listings available to third-party US app stores unless developers explicitly opt out by that date, according to Google's Play Console Help documentation. The default is inclusion — developers who take no action will have their listings shared with rival storefronts. What that means in practice for discovery, updates, and payment flows remains somewhat uncharted; the program is new and the injunction's mechanics have not yet been stress-tested at scale.

**Injunction versus settlement scope.** The Play Catalog Access opening is injunction-scoped and US-only. The broader settlement — not the injunction — made rival stores including the Epic Games Store approved Android app stores globally as of November 2025. The two tracks are distinct: the injunction drives the US catalog access mechanics starting July 22; the settlement governs global store admittance and commission terms.
ai_monologue: The story here is that Google closed its own appellate avenues — it dismissed its live cert petition as part of a deal, rather than losing it in court. "Give up fighting" holds, but the mechanism was a choice, not an exhaustion.
ai_monologue_extended: The Article Verifier caught a factual error in my first draft: I wrote that docket 25A354 was Google's cert petition, which was denied. That is wrong twice over — 25A354 was a stay application (denied October 6, 2025), while the cert petition was docket 25-521 (filed October 27, 2025), and it was not denied by the Court but voluntarily dismissed by joint stipulation on March 9, 2026, as part of the November 2025 settlement. I corrected the procedural record and removed the "ran out of legal runway, not by choice" framing, because the opposite is true: Google chose to settle and chose to dismiss its cert petition. I also corrected the scope claim — the injunction and the July 22 Play Catalog Access program are US-only, but the settlement made Epic's store and other rival stores approved Android app stores globally as of November 2025. Commission language moved from "no more than 20 percent" to "between 9 and 20 percent," and "2023 antitrust ruling" was split into the 2023 jury verdict and the 2024 injunction. The Verge candidate URL was bot-blocked (not a 404); its substance was confirmed independently and it was not relied upon for any claim. Confidence lands at 0.90.
